$comment: CROSS-IMPLEMENTATION WIRE CONTRACT — keep this file byte-identical in both repos:
nest-auth/conformance/wire-contract.json
rust-auth/conformance/wire-contract.json
Both libraries can back the same deployment and share one Redis, so these values are a
contract between them rather than an implementation detail of either. Each repo has a
test that reads this file and asserts its own implementation matches, so a change on one
side turns that side's suite red immediately instead of surfacing months later as
sessions, lockouts, and reset links that silently miss each other in production.
Changing a value here is a breaking change to the shared keyspace. Do it in both repos in
the same change, and only with a migration story for data already written in the old form.
`version` names the contract a RELEASE of nest-auth ships. It moves once per release that
changes the contract, never once per change: an edit to a version no release has shipped yet
stays inside that version, and rust-auth reads it the same way.
Every string in this file, key or value, must be well-formed Unicode, because a parser that builds
well-formed strings (serde_json is one) rejects a lone surrogate escape and loses the whole file.
A case that needs an ill-formed string states it as UTF-16 code units beside its `case`, for
example `unpairedSurrogateCodeUnits: [55296]`, and each library's test builds the string itself.
The identifier-hashing key both sides derive from the identifier secret, and one
identifier keyed with it. The identifier secret is the `identifierKey` option when it is
set and the JWT secret otherwise, so pinning `identifierKey` to the JWT secret's value
keeps every derived name where it is across a rotation of the JWT secret. Three things
are pinned at once: the ':' separator between label and
secret, the SHA-256, and the fact that the HMAC is keyed with the hex TEXT of the digest
rather than its raw bytes. Any of the three drifting produces different Redis keys for
every lockout, OTP, resend cooldown, MFA setup, and anti-replay record.
The same vector continues into the OTP record. The stored value is never the code
itself — six digits is a keyspace of a million, reversible offline from a Redis dump —
but the hmac-sha256 of `{identifier}:{code}` under that derived key. Pinned here
because both implementations write and compare the SAME `otp:` record, so a drift is
not a parse error on the other side: it is every code minted on one backend failing to
verify on the other, in both directions.
hmacKeyDerivation.label: bymax-auth:hmac-key:v1

$comment: The prefix each keyspace uses, under the configured namespace: {namespace}:{prefix}:{id}.
The dashboard and platform planes are deliberately separate — a consumer's user ids and
admin ids come from different repositories and may collide, so one shared index let a
revoke on one plane log the other out.
`ra:` is the recent-authentication marker: presence means the account completed a REAL
authentication within RECENT_AUTH_TTL_SECONDS (300). Written only where a session is
BORN — never on a refresh rotation, which proves possession of a token rather than of a
credential. That asymmetry is the whole value: a stolen session can be rotated forever
and never make the mark fresh again. It gates enrolling MFA on an account with no local
password, where there is nothing to re-prove and a stolen access token was otherwise
enough to enrol a factor the attacker holds — irreversibly, since disable and
regenerate both demand a live TOTP and the reset flow refuses a passwordless account.
Keyed hmac_sha256('{plane}:{userId}') like every other user-derived key, and
plane-bound so ids colliding across the two repositories cannot satisfy each other.
The account-status cache both libraries read from one Redis. A deployment that runs both
behind one store shares it, so the key, the value and the invalidation order are part of the
contract: a delete that stops matching raises nothing and merely defers a suspension or a
verification by one TTL, and nothing else would notice.
Two entries per account: `us` holds the status string, `uev` holds whether the address is
verified. Both are keyed by the HMAC of the tenant-scoped DASHBOARD user subject, exactly like
every other key that names an account (`userSubjectDerivedKeys`). The tenant is in the subject
because a repository id is unique only within a tenant; the HMAC is there because the store is
shared and readable, and an account identifier written into a key in the clear is disclosed to
anyone who can list it. The cache is dashboard-only: the platform status check is uncached, so
there is no platform subject to derive and a dashboard account can never share a key with a
platform one.
**Keys of any other shape are not read.** A backend that keys these entries differently, for
example by the tenant and the user id percent-encoded in the clear, names other keys than this
one. Both entries are TTL'd cache values, so nothing needs migrating: the first read misses and
refills. Running two shapes side by side is bounded by `ttl`: an invalidation issued by one
side deletes a key the other does not read, so a changed status can be served stale for up to
one TTL, and each account costs one extra repository read. Drain the other shape before this
one serves to avoid even that.
userStatusCache.userSubject: the dashboard arm of userSubjectPreimages; this cache has no platform counterpart
userStatusCache.hmacKey: the identifier-HMAC key of hmacKeyDerivation, and the vectors below use its pinned derivedKeyHex
userStatusCache.statusValue: the status string exactly as the repository returned it; not case-folded and not trimmed (the blocked-status comparison canonicalizes at read time)
userStatusCache.emailVerifiedRead: read, and written on a miss, only when email verification is required; otherwise only the status entry exists

ttl.appliesTo: every entry written on a miss, set with the same value

userStatusCache.fill: a miss on the status entry, or on the verified entry when it is read, resolves both from one tenant-scoped repository read and writes both back
userStatusCache.invalidateOrderWhy: the verified entry is deleted first so that a failure between the two deletes leaves the entry whose staleness only costs a repository read; a stale `0` would lock a just-verified account out until it expires

$comment: The workspace-membership cache both libraries read and write on one Redis. A deployment that
runs both behind one store shares it, so the subjects, the keys, the value and the ORDER of the
version reads are part of the contract: a version bump issued by one side that names a
different key than the other reads raises nothing and serves a removed member's role until
the entry expires.
Access to a workspace needs an ACTIVE membership of an ACTIVE workspace. Any other state reads
as 'not a member', so a caller cannot tell a workspace it may not enter from one that does
not exist (`auth.workspace_not_found`).
Two subjects, both length-prefixed in UTF-8 BYTES for the reason `userSubjectPreimages` gives:
a bare `:` between free-form identifiers is not injective, and a UTF-16 length would derive
different keys from a UTF-8 one for the first accented identifier. Identifiers are used as
given: there is NO Unicode normalisation, so a composed and a decomposed spelling of the same
text are different identifiers with different digests. The user id is last and unprefixed
because nothing follows it. Every key HMACs its subject with the identifier key of
`hmacKeyDerivation`, so no identifier is written into the keyspace in the clear. No other
preimage under that key starts with `wsp:` or `wms:`, so these subjects cannot collide with
the account subjects.
Three keys. `wsv` and `wmv` are version counters; `wm` holds the cached answer under BOTH
versions. THE ORDER IS THE REQUIREMENT: a reader reads `wsv`, then `wmv`, then the entry named
by those two values, then, on a miss, the repositories, and writes the entry under the versions
it read FIRST. A change that lands after the version reads moves a counter, so the refill sits
under a key nobody reads and is never served. Reading all three in one atomic step is an
optimisation, not a requirement: an implementation may issue the reads as separate
single-key commands, or pipeline them, provided the order holds. A multi-key read across the
three keys is not required and is not portable to a store that shards by key.
What the order guarantees: a read that BEGINS after a bump has returned never serves an entry
written before that bump, because the bump is committed before it returns and the reader reads
the counters first. A read that overlaps a bump may be answered from the state before it, as a
request that finished a moment earlier would be; separate reads do not make a read that
straddles a bump fresh, and the contract does not ask them to.
A counter value is never reused while an entry bearing it can live. A counter that expires
restarts at 1 on its next bump, and an entry still alive under 1 would be current again. A
retention longer than the entry lifetime is not enough on its own, since an entry can be written
in the last moment of a counter's retention, or after the counter expired between the version
read and the write. So a fill writes only if both counters still hold the versions it read (an
absent counter counts as 0), and in the same step it extends every counter that exists to the
retention. A counter that does not exist is left absent: it reads as 0, and a read never creates
a counter. A fill that finds a counter moved writes nothing, which also skips an entry nobody
could read.
A writer changes the repository FIRST and bumps the counter after, and a failed bump is an
error: a change is never reported as invalidated when it was not. A bump is INCR followed by
EXPIRE, on every bump, so a counter always carries its retention; nest-auth issues both in one
atomic step.
nest-auth runs the read and the bump as Lua scripts, so it supports a standalone Redis and
Sentinel only, like every other multi-key script in this library (its Redis Cluster position is
documented in the technical specification).
The cache is advisory. When Redis is unreachable a reader answers from the repositories and
writes nothing. The repository reads the cache is filled from must come from the primary or
be read-your-writes: a lagging replica would cache a removed member as present under the new
version.
A counter evicted under memory pressure restarts at 0, which can make an entry written under
an earlier 0:0 readable again for up to its TTL. This is the same exposure the token-epoch
counters have; run the store with a no-eviction policy for the auth keyspace.
workspaceMembershipCache.hmacKey: the identifier-HMAC key of hmacKeyDerivation, and the vectors below use its pinned derivedKeyHex
workspaceMembershipCache.absentVersion: a counter that does not exist reads as the text '0'
workspaceMembershipCache.entryRule: only an active membership of an active workspace is cached; a missing, suspended or inactive answer is never cached, and an entry whose status is not 'active' is read as a miss

ttl.zero: disables the cache: every request reads the repositories

workspaceMembershipCache.versionRetentionWhy: a counter must outlive every entry written under it, or it restarts at 0 and revives a stale entry; the value is TOKEN_EPOCH_RETENTION_SECONDS
workspaceMembershipCache.bump: INCR the counter, then EXPIRE it to versionRetentionSeconds, atomically and on every bump
workspaceMembershipCache.workspaceWideEvents: deleting, scheduling the deletion of, restoring or suspending a workspace bumps the workspace version; a change to one membership bumps that membership's version only
workspaceMembershipCache.entryRead: the entry is a JSON object that is read by PARSING, never compared as text; a value that is not valid JSON, whose role is not a string, or whose status is not 'active' is a miss
workspaceMembershipCache.blankParts: a tenantId, workspaceId or userId that is not a string, is empty, or is only whitespace is refused before any key is derived; no key is ever built from a blank part

$comment: Run by both implementations against a store and two repositories. `repository` is the state the repositories hold at that step; `expect.answer` is the role returned or null; `expect.source` is where the answer came from; `expect.cachedUnder` is the versions of the entry that exists afterwards for this member, or null when there is no entry under the CURRENT versions; `expect.absentUnder` lists versions under which no entry may exist afterwards. Versions start at 0:0. `concurrentBump` names a counter bumped after the reader has read the versions and the repositories and before the fill; `dropCounter` removes a counter, standing for its expiry, and the counter then reads as 0. `counterLoss` runs on a fresh store.

Starts from a store with no entries. A fill that finds a counter moved writes nothing, and a counter that is lost reads as 0 and is recreated at 1 by the next bump, so no entry written before the loss can be read after it, on a store where no entry is alive under a value the counter will restart at; an entry that is, is the documented eviction exposure.

workspaceMembershipCache.entryRefreshesCounters: a fill writes the entry only if both counters still hold the versions it read (absent counts as 0), and in the same step extends every existing counter to the retention

$comment: The session a grace recovery produces is written in ONE atomic step, gated on the
per-user session index still existing.
The rotation script moved the session-index bookkeeping inside itself precisely to close
the window in which 'log out everywhere' could miss a session a rotation had just
minted. The GRACE arm was left outside it: the script returned the recovered record and
the engine wrote the session keys several round trips later. A revoke-all landing in
between — a password reset, an MFA enable, a ban compensation — swept an index that did
not yet contain the session, so the session survived a revocation the user was told had
happened, and its access token, signed afterwards, carried the POST-bump epoch and
verified. An attacker holding a stolen token gets one grace-eligible token per rotation,
so they can keep a continuous stream of these in flight for as long as the reset takes.
The witness is the per-user session index: the revoke-all transaction deletes that set
once it has removed every member, so its absence is exactly 'a revoke-all has run', and
the successor the grace pointer named is itself indexed, so a legitimate recovery always
finds it present. The family index is re-checked in the same step, because the engine's
own EXISTS ran before the write and a revoke-family in between would be undone by it.
A refused write must surface as auth.refresh_token_invalid: the grace pointer is already
consumed, so there is nothing to retry against, and the revocation is what the caller
must obey. Both implementations must gate on the same witness, or one of them keeps the
window the other closed.
graceRecoveryWrite.gate: EXISTS {sessionIndex}, and EXISTS {familyIndex}:{familyId} when the record names a family

$comment: The dashboard arm carries a LENGTH PREFIX because a bare `:` between two free-form
components is not injective. Both halves may legitimately contain the delimiter — the DTO
charset deliberately admits a tenant id like `acme.eu-west-1:prod`, and a composite
`tenant:user` subject is a documented shape — so without the prefix
(tenantId 'acme:prod', userId 'u1') and (tenantId 'acme', userId 'prod:u1') both render
`dashboard:acme:prod:u1`. Two unrelated tenants would then share ONE session index, ONE
token epoch, one set of MFA store keys and one recovery-code single-use claim: the
cross-tenant revocation this contract exists to prevent, reintroduced through the
delimiter, plus one tenant able to spend another's recovery code.
The prefix counts UTF-8 BYTES, not characters. JavaScript's String.length counts UTF-16
code units and Rust's str::len() counts bytes: `açaí` is 4 by one measure and 6 by the
other, so a character count would agree across the two implementations for ASCII and
derive different keys on the first accented tenant id. Rust uses `tenant_id.len()`,
TypeScript uses `Buffer.byteLength(tenantId, 'utf8')`.
The platform arm has one component after the plane and nothing to disambiguate, so it is
left unprefixed — changing it would move a keyspace for no gain.
The subject EVERY MFA store key and MFA failure counter below is derived from. One
definition rather than eight copies: eight keys share this shape, and a copy that drifts is
a key that silently stops matching the one the other implementation derives.
The tenant is part of the dashboard arm because neither library may assume the consumer's
user ids are unique ACROSS tenants — `findById` takes a tenant precisely because they may
not be, and a host that numbers users per tenant gives every tenant a user `1`. Keyed on
`{plane}:{userId}` alone, two tenants' accounts shared all five store keys and all three
failure counters. The counters were the worst of the eight and it is not close: the other
five cost a collision between two accounts that happen to share an id, while the counters
cost a CREDENTIAL-FREE CROSS-TENANT LOCKOUT — failures against one tenant's user spent
another tenant's budget and a success on either side cleared the other's. That is not the
per-subscriber-account rate limiting NIST SP 800-63B requires, and it is the same bug the
`identifierPreimages` block below already documents one level up, where a tenant literally
named `platform` collided with the platform plane and locked an operator out of the console.
That fix landed for the login counter and stopped there.
The platform arm carries NO tenant segment: its admins are cross-tenant and have none, and
an invented value would become a lookup key. Both implementations derive the shape from the
PLANE, not from whether a tenant was supplied, so a caller that passes one on the platform
plane cannot move the preimage off `platform:{userId}`.
The dashboard MFA temp token carries `tenantId` for this reason. A challenge token without
it is REFUSED, not defaulted: RFC 8725 §3.9 sets the absent-means-reject pattern, §3.12
requires validation rules that reject a token of the wrong kind, and ASVS 5.0 6.6.2 requires
the out-of-band token be bound to the authentication request that generated it. Falling back
would leave the unscoped derivation reachable by omitting one optional field.

mfaTransitionLock.value: a per-call nonce (16 CSPRNG bytes, hex) — the release compares against it
$comment: Serializes MFA state transitions for one account. Every transition rewrites a single
repository record carrying mfaEnabled, the encrypted secret and the recovery-code
digests TOGETHER, and the update replaces all three wholesale — the repository is the
host's and offers no compare-and-set — so interleaved transitions are last-write-wins.
Three ways that bit: two challenges spending DIFFERENT recovery codes each write the
full list minus their own, resurrecting the loser's code; a challenge that read the list
before a regenerate and splices after it restores the whole replaced set; and a challenge
that splices after a disable completes writes mfaEnabled back with the pre-disable
secret. The recoveryCodeClaim below does not cover any of them — it is keyed on the code,
so it serializes two attempts at the SAME code and nothing else.
A caller that cannot take the lock is refused with auth.mfa_state_conflict rather than
made to wait. The TTL is short because the lock is released explicitly; it bounds only a
process that dies mid-transition, and an account whose MFA is briefly unchangeable is
worse than a window this narrow.
The release must be a compare-and-delete against that nonce, in ONE step. The TTL is
short and a transition calls into the consumer's repository twice, so a run that
overruns has already lost the lock: deleting the key unconditionally then removes
whichever transition holds it now, and a third caller enters beside the second. A GET
followed by a DEL does not express the check either — the key can be retaken between
the two round trips, which is the interleaving the nonce exists to catch.
Both implementations must derive the same key, or the two halves of one deployment
serialize against different locks and the property is lost.
Consuming a recovery code is a read-modify-write against the CONSUMER's user repository:
the challenge reads the whole array, removes one entry, and writes the rest back. Two
challenges landing together both read the array, both match, and both write — one code
mints two sessions, which is the one property a recovery code has. Neither library can fix
that in the repository, whose atomicity is the consumer's to define, so both claim the code
with SET NX in the store they share. First claim wins; every other reads as an invalid code.
Same construction as the TOTP anti-replay marker: the key discloses neither the user nor the
code, and binding the plane stops a dashboard user and a platform admin with the same id
burning each other's codes. Deliberately short-lived — it serializes a race, it is not the
durable record of consumption, and outliving the repository write would turn a failed write
into a code the account can see but can never use.
The keys that derive from `userSubjectPreimages`. A contract detects drift only in what it
lists, so every key that names an ACCOUNT rather than a token belongs here.
`sessionIndex` and `tokenEpoch` were the last two to join, and they were the two that made
the preimage's own argument concrete. They were keyed on the BARE user id: `sess:{userId}`
and `ep:{userId}`. Neither library may assume the consumer's user ids are unique across
tenants — `findById` takes a tenant precisely because they may not be — so on a deployment
that numbers users per tenant, suspending or deleting `t1/u1` swept the sessions and bumped
the token epoch of `t2/u1`. A credential-free cross-tenant revocation, reachable by anyone
who can get an account suspended in their own tenant.
The bare id was also an account identifier in the clear in a store both libraries read,
which is the second reason every key here is an HMAC and not a bare digest: a user id
carries too little entropy for a plain hash to hide it, exactly as an address does.
The platform arm keeps no tenant segment, because `userSubject` drops it there — its admins
are cross-tenant and have none.
**This change has no compatibility path and needs both libraries in the same release.** A
backend on the old shape writes `sess:{userId}` while one on the new shape reads
`sess:{hmac}`: sessions stay alive and unswept, and a revoke-all misses them.
**That also forbids a ROLLING deploy of one library against itself.** Drain the pods on the
old release before the new ones serve. The MFA keyspace is where this bites rather than the
session one: the transition lock that serializes a read-modify-write on the recovery-code
list is keyed by this same subject, so two pods that disagree about the subject take
different locks and do not exclude each other at all. The `rcu:` claim is keyed by it too,
so the same recovery code can be claimed once on each side and then spent by two
unserialized writes. Neither library carries a fallback for the previous tenant-scoped
preimage: a deliberate choice, because a fallback is compatibility weight for a deployment
that a cutover removes the need for, and the cutover is the stronger position.
**A live keyspace must be MIGRATED, not dropped.** Deleting the old keys is unsafe in both
directions, and each direction is a hole rather than an inconvenience.
**The dashboard migration is a FAN-OUT, not a rename: one old key becomes N new ones.** The
old keys are tenant-blind — `ep:{userId}` and `sess:{userId}` name a bare user id — which is
the very defect this change removes, so a single old key served EVERY tenant that has a user
with that id. Each of those pairs derives its own key now. An operator who copies an old key
to one derived key and drops it has migrated one tenant and silently reset all the others,
which is the hole described below rather than a partial migration. Enumerate the tenants
that user id appears in and write every one of them. On the PLATFORM plane the mapping is
1:1 — its subject carries no tenant — so the fan-out is a dashboard-only obligation.
Deleting an old `ep:{userId}` does not expire the tokens it revoked. The reader answers 0
for an absent key, and under 0 the `stamped < epoch` test is false for EVERY token — so a
password reset, an MFA reset or a sign-out-everywhere that had already invalidated an
access token is undone, and that token works again for the rest of its lifetime. Epochs
must be COPIED to EVERY derived key the old one served — each with at least the old value
and at least the remainder of its TTL — and only then dropped. Missing one tenant is not a
smaller version of dropping the key: for that tenant it IS dropping the key. An epoch may
never move backwards.
Deleting an old `sess:{userId}` does not end the sessions it listed. Its `rt:`/`rp:` members
outlive it and become unreachable: a later revoke-all reads the new, empty index, finds
nothing to delete and reports success while those refresh tokens keep rotating. Either
re-add the members under the derived index keys, or delete the member keys and their detail
records BEFORE dropping the index. The second costs a forced re-login and is the safer of
the two; the first preserves sessions and must be done atomically per user.
Re-adding is where the fan-out bites hardest, because the old index MIXES tenants: its
members are the sessions of every tenant's user with that id, and dropping them all into one
derived index would hand one tenant another's live sessions — a worse outcome than the
collision being fixed, since it is now a listable, revocable cross-tenant handle. Partition
instead: each member names an `rt:`/`rp:` record that carries its OWN `tenantId`, so read the
record, derive that pair's index, and place the member there. A member whose record is gone
is already dead and is dropped rather than guessed at.
**Both obligations apply to the PLATFORM twins, `pep:{userId}` and `psess:{userId}`**, which
this change relocates identically. They are the easier pair to forget and the worse pair to
get wrong: a platform epoch left behind revalidates previously revoked ADMIN tokens, and a
platform index left behind hides an admin's live refresh sessions from revoke-all. The
platform subject carries no tenant segment, but the HMAC relocates the key all the same, so
an operator with no tenants still owes both steps on both planes.
The preimage each plane HMACs into its `lf:` counter key. The identity PLANE is part of
it, not just the tenant: without the `dashboard:` segment a tenant whose id is literally
`platform` produced a byte-identical identifier to the platform plane's own, so five
unauthenticated dashboard logins against an operator's address locked that operator out
of the console — repeatably, without the platform surface ever being touched — and a
successful one cleared their lockout mid-attack. `tenantId` comes from the request body
whenever no resolver is configured, which is the default, so it was attacker-chosen.
The OTP identifier is deliberately NOT plane-scoped and keeps the bare
`{tenantId}:{email}` shape: its keyspace is already purpose-scoped (`otp:{purpose}:`),
the platform plane has no OTP flow, and moving it would split records in flight.
The invitee index takes the canonicalized address alone — the tenant is already a literal
segment of that key. It is an HMAC and not a bare digest for the reason all of these are:
an address carries too little entropy for a plain SHA-256 to hide it.
The two workspace-invitation preimages use the same length prefix, in UTF-8 bytes, for the
reason `userSubjectPreimages` gives, and leave the last component unprefixed because nothing
follows it. The pending set of a workspace is keyed on the workspace subject of
`workspaceMembershipCache`. None of the three starts with a prefix any other preimage uses.
The length bounds every request DTO applies to a shared field, held identical by both
implementations. They matter beyond tidiness: an unbounded field on a public route is a
free byte sink to carry, parse and log, and a bound that differs between the two backends
means the same request is accepted by one and refused by the other — for a deployment that
runs both behind one address, that is a difference nobody can explain from the outside.
The password bounds split deliberately. Setting a password enforces the policy minimum;
PROVING one (login, or the current-password re-proof) floors at 1, because the credential
may predate whatever the policy says today and a policy floor on a login door refuses a
legitimate holder with a validation error while telling an unauthenticated caller what the
policy is, before any key derivation runs.
Every length bound on text a USER SUBMITS, on a request field or on the service-side check behind
it, counts Unicode CODE POINTS and not UTF-16 units, as validator.js isLength does by subtracting
surrogate pairs: an emoji is one. A string of 120 emoji meets a bound of 120. Store-key and
storage bounds are not user text and may count bytes by design.

memberUserId.$comment: The user id of a workspace member, in a path segment or a body field, with no control character.

workspaceName.$comment: The display name of a workspace. The bound and the control-character rule apply to the value as submitted, before any trimming: a name over 120 characters as submitted, or carrying a control character anywhere, is refused with 400 auth.validation naming the field name. The name is then stored trimmed, and one that is blank after trimming is refused the same way.

pageLimit.$comment: The `limit` query parameter of a paginated list, a whole number written in decimal digits without a leading zero (`5`, not `05`). A value outside 1 to 100, or not written that way, is refused with 400 auth.validation naming the field limit, a present but empty `limit=` included; it is never clamped. The cursor is opaque, 1 to 4096 characters (an empty `cursor=` is refused) with no control character, and says only where the next page starts: the tenant and the workspace of a list always come from the credential and the route. 4096 is sized for the longest cursor a repository can issue from ids, tenants and key parts of 128 code points (a code point is counted once, an emoji included) and an owner role the `workspaceOwnerRole` rule admits, which is 2306 characters in the format nest-auth's adapters use; the format of a cursor is private to each repository and is not part of this contract.

pathParameters.$comment: A path parameter that is over its bound, blank, or carries a control character is refused with 400 auth.validation naming the parameter, ahead of authorization. The workspace guard runs first, so when both `workspaceId` and another parameter are bad only `workspaceId` is reported. A well-formed parameter that names nothing, or a workspace the caller may not see, is the identical 404 auth.workspace_not_found. `Blank` means only JS `\s` whitespace; the control-character rule is a separate pattern. A workspace id is always a library-generated UUID, so it can never be `invitations`, and the static `workspaces/invitations/...` routes cannot shadow a workspace.

$comment: The order of the checks on the reset-password route, which decides the answer for a request
that fails more than one of them. It is the same in both libraries, so a client sees one
behaviour whichever one serves it.
steps: 1. classify the proof without spending it: more than one proof, none, or one the configured passwordReset.method does not accept answers auth.password_reset_token_invalid, whatever the new password is
2. judge the new password (the policy floor, then the breach screen): auth.validation for a password under the floor, auth.password_compromised for a known one

3. spend the proof: auth.password_reset_token_invalid for a token proof that is not valid; auth.otp_invalid for EVERY OTP failure (a wrong code, an absent record, an expired one and an exhausted attempt ceiling are indistinguishable)
passwordResetOrder.reason: A request with no usable proof never reaches the password policy, so an unproven caller cannot drive the breach screen (an outbound query when a host wires one), and a refused password never consumes a single-use proof.

$comment: Where a refresh token may arrive and what each place accepts. The bound is the
`opaqueToken` bound in `requestFieldBounds`; no token either library mints is longer.
A value refused here is refused before any store lookup.
refreshTokenInput.body: a string of 1 to 2048 characters; a missing field or a JSON null is no token; anything else present (not a string, empty, longer) is refused with 400 auth.validation naming the field refreshToken
refreshTokenInput.cookie: a value over 2048 characters is refused with 400 auth.validation naming the field refreshToken, except on logout, which reads it as no token (204, the auth cookies cleared, no refresh session touched, and a presented access token is still blacklisted); an empty cookie is no token; under tokenDelivery both, a cookie over 2048 on logout is read as absent, so a valid refreshToken in the body is the token that applies and its session is revoked

$comment: Index members are FULL key suffixes, not bare hashes. The member has to name its own
keyspace: an atomic revoke rebuilds keys from members, and a bare hash cannot say whether
it is a live session or a rotation grace pointer. Grace pointers are members too, which is
what lets a revoke-all also kill a token that was rotated away but is still in its window.
The membership is maintained BY THE ROTATION SCRIPT, not by the caller afterwards. Done
after the script it left a window between the consume and the SADD in which a revoke-all
sweep could miss the session the rotation had just minted — leaving it alive, and still
rotating, after a revocation the user was told had happened. Inside the script the two
serialize. Either backend rotating the other's sessions must keep it there.
A refresh-token FAMILY is one login lineage: minted at login, inherited unchanged by
every rotation, and the unit reuse detection revokes. Unlike the session index, its
members are BARE hashes — a family only ever tracks live refresh sessions, so the
keyspace is implied and does not need to be carried in the member.
What a presented refresh token can be, and what each outcome does. These are behaviours
rather than bytes, but they have to agree: the two backends share the markers below, so
one side treating a replay as recoverable while the other treats it as theft would make
the reaction depend on which backend the request happened to reach.
rotationSemantics.graceWindow: single-shot — the pointer is consumed on use, so one captured token cannot mint a session repeatedly inside the window
rotationSemantics.graceRequiresLiveFamily: a recovery is refused once its family index is gone, so a pointer that outlived a revocation cannot resurrect the lineage
rotationSemantics.reuseSignal: a consumed token replayed after its grace window closed, detected by the consumed-family marker outliving the pointer
rotationSemantics.reuseReaction: revoke the whole family (every live descendant of that login) and reject the request; the user's other logins are untouched
rotationSemantics.legacySessionWithoutFamily: skips all family bookkeeping and can never trip reuse detection

$comment: Timestamp encoding differs per record and is NOT uniform — this is the trap. The session
DETAIL uses epoch milliseconds because the reader guards on `typeof === 'number'` and
evicts a member whose detail fails to parse; everything else uses an ISO-8601 string.

refreshSession.familyId: omitted from the record entirely when empty, never written as an empty string
refreshSession.familyCreatedAt: iso8601-string; the FAMILY's birth, carried unchanged through every rotation — distinct from createdAt, which is this session's own and resets on each one. Omitted alongside familyId on a legacy record, which is then not subject to the absolute lifetime cap.
refreshSession.mfaVerified: boolean; written ONLY as `true`, when the session was established through the MFA challenge, and omitted otherwise — never written as `false`. Read strictly: only a JSON boolean `true` is verified, so a record without the field (a legacy record, or one opened without the challenge) and any other value read as false. Carried unchanged through every rotation and every grace-window recovery, on both planes.
refreshSession.$comment: mfaEnabled must survive rotation: the MFA gate refuses only when mfaEnabled && !mfaVerified, so losing it turns one refresh into a silent second-factor bypass. mfaVerified must survive it too, from the other side: no route lets an authenticated session re-acquire the claim, so a rotation that does not carry it forward locks every MFA user out of every route behind the gate once the access token ages out.

invitation.$comment: Consumption is a single-use GETDEL, so a record the reader rejects is destroyed rather than retried — a missing field loses the invitation outright.

invitationIndex.value: the invitation's token hash (lowercase hex), pointing at its `inv:` record
$comment: The one handle the issuing side has on a pending invitation: the record itself is keyed by
the hash of a token only the invitee's mailbox ever held, so without this nobody can name a
pending invitation, let alone withdraw one. Carries the invitation's TTL, so the pair expires
together. The email is hashed rather than stored in the clear — a dump of the keyspace must
not enumerate who a tenant has been inviting. Re-inviting an address supersedes the previous
invitation through this key: two live tokens for one invitee is two chances for an
intercepted link, and a revoke would only ever reach the newest.
The address is HMAC'd, not plainly digested: an address carries too little entropy for a
bare SHA-256 to hide it, and this key is the one handle anyone reading a keyspace dump has
on who a tenant has been inviting. The preimage is the canonicalized address alone — the
tenant is already a literal segment of the key.

wsTicket.tenantId: omitted from the record entirely when the ticket is not tenant-scoped
wsTicket.jti: string, non-empty; the jti of the access token that minted the ticket — the key of the per-token blacklist rv:{jti}
wsTicket.epoch: non-negative integer; the token epoch stamped on the minting access token, 0 when it carried none
wsTicket.$comment: A verified-identity SNAPSHOT, never a token: no signature, no expiry of its own. The socket it authorizes cannot be turned back into a session. Redemption is a single-use GETDEL, so a captured upgrade URL is worthless once the socket opens. jti and epoch are identifiers, not credentials: they are the two keys the revocation channels are read by, so redemption is refused exactly when the minting token would be — blacklisted, or stamped below the user's current epoch. A record missing either, or carrying them malformed, is not a ticket.

logoutPending.key: lp:{sha256(refreshToken)} on the dashboard plane, plp:{sha256(refreshToken)} on the platform plane
logoutPending.tenantId: omitted from the record entirely when the session record carried none, always on the platform plane
logoutPending.ttl: the configured access-token lifetime in seconds, rounded up, and never less than 300
logoutPending.writer: only a logout attempt that FAILED a revocation write and had read its owner from the live refresh session; best effort, written before the failure is raised; never written on the success path and never by a retry that read only the marker
logoutPending.reader: a logout whose refresh session is gone reads the owner from this record instead
logoutPending.claim: a logout that completes with no failure removes the key; when the owner came from this record the afterLogout hook fires only if that removal removed the key, so racing retries announce once; when the owner came from the live session the hook fires regardless and any stale record is removed
logoutPending.guarantee: exactly-once for sequential retries; at-least-once when attempts of one logout run concurrently (attempts that all read the live session each announce on completing, and a failed attempt slower than a successful one can write its marker after that one cleared it, leaving a marker a later retry claims)
logoutPending.$comment: A hint to whom a logout belonged, never a credential and never a session: it cannot authenticate anything, and the owner it names was read from the library's own session record, not from a token's claims. It exists because a failed attempt deletes the refresh session whatever else it could not write, so the retry that completes the logout would otherwise have no record to say whose it was.

$comment: The pending address change, held under a token that is mailed to the NEW address and
nowhere else — proving the requester controls it before it becomes the account's
address. Consumed with GETDEL, so a link works exactly once.
`newEmail` is stored ALREADY NORMALIZED (trimmed, lowercased), because the uniqueness
check at confirm time compares it against the repository the same way login does. The
old address is not stored: it is read from the account at confirm time, so a record
that outlives an intervening change still notifies wherever the account actually is.
`passwordFingerprint` binds the token to the password in force when it was minted,
exactly as the reset context does. An attacker who plants a change request and waits
loses it the moment the victim changes their password — which is the first thing a
victim does. An ABSENT field is read as 'no binding' and accepted, so a rolling deploy
does not break the changes already in flight.
emailChangeContext.passwordFingerprint: sha256 of the account's password hash when the token was minted, or the empty string when the account had none.

passwordResetContext.passwordFingerprint: sha256 of the account's password hash at the moment the token was minted, or the empty string when the account had none. Several reset tokens can be alive at once, and completing one used to leave the rest valid — the wrong end state exactly when it matters, since a victim resetting BECAUSE an attacker read a link from their mailbox had not closed the link the attacker read. The binding makes the first completed reset invalidate all of them, with no per-user index to keep in step. An ABSENT field is read as 'no binding' and accepted, so a rolling deploy does not break the resets already in flight.

oauthState.workspaceInvitation: The lowercase hex SHA-256 of the workspace invitation token the flow was started with, written only when it was; the raw token is never stored. A record carrying it as anything but 64 lowercase hex characters is refused as corrupt, and one without it is an ordinary sign-in.
oauthState.$comment: The record of an OAuth flow between its start and its callback, read and deleted in one step by the callback. Both libraries read the same record.

$comment: The shapes of the credentials themselves. Both sides must mint and accept the same ones
or a session started on one backend cannot continue on the other.
credentialFormats.passwordHash: PHC — see the passwordHashFormat section, which pins it by vector
credentialFormats.totpSecretAtRest: aes-256-gcm over the BASE32 TEXT of the secret
credentialFormats.recoveryCodeDigest: hex hmac-sha256 of the code under the derived identifier key
credentialFormats.otpRecordCode: hex hmac-sha256 of `{identifier}:{code}` under the derived identifier key
credentialFormats.wsTicket: 64 lowercase hex characters (32 CSPRNG bytes), single-use, at most 30 s and never beyond the minting access token's own expiry
credentialFormats.apiKey: `{prefix}_{keyId}_{secret}` — prefix `bak` by default, keyId a lowercase canonical UUID, secret 43 base64url characters (32 CSPRNG bytes); stored only as the hex hmac-sha256 of the secret under the pepper

$comment: The stored password hash, pinned by known-answer vector rather than by description.
credentialFormats.passwordHash used to read 'self-describing: the parameters the hash was
written under travel with it'. BOTH sides satisfied that while writing mutually unreadable
strings — nest-auth wrote scrypt:N:r:p:{saltHex}:{derivedHex}, rust-auth wrote PHC. Neither
could verify the other's, and because verification is total the failure surfaced as
auth.invalid_credentials rather than as a parse error: five correct attempts by the owner
tripped the SHARED brute-force counter and locked the account out of both backends. Prose
each side can satisfy alone is not a contract. A vector each side must verify against the
other's real output is. Nothing below is hand-written — every string is emitted output.
There is no compatibility path and no second encoding. Both libraries are new and have
never backed a deployment, so a reader for an older shape would be a branch in the
credential-verification core serving a corpus that does not exist — which is where an
unused branch is most expensive. A hash either parses as PHC or is refused.
passwordHashFormat.b64: PHC 'B64': the standard base64 alphabet with padding stripped. NOT base64url — a hash written with '-' or '_' is one the sibling parser rejects.
passwordHashFormat.params: read by name, never by position: ln, r and p may appear in any order, and a repeated key is refused rather than resolved
passwordHashFormat.derivedKeyLengthBytes: carried implicitly by the field's own length; 10..=64 accepted (the bounds of rust-auth's password_hash::Output). nest-auth writes 64, rust-auth writes 32, and each verifies the other under the length it reads.
passwordHashFormat.needsRehash: each vector's flag is evaluated with the deployment configured at exactly the cost that vector records (ln=14, r=8, p=1). Against a higher configured cost every vector is stale, which would make the flag say nothing about the encoding.
passwordHashFormat.rehashTriggers: a recorded cost below the configured one. NOT the derived-key length: the two implementations write different lengths (64 and 32), both carry it in the hash, and treating the sibling's as stale would rehash every record on every crossing and never converge.

vectors.note: 64-byte derived key — the maximum password_hash::Output can represent

$comment: Both backends enforce these with a Redis fixed-window counter shared across instances; the
key shape under the rl: prefix is per implementation (route naming is not shared), so one
client served by both libraries gets a budget from each.
The per-IP limit each auth route is served under, as `requests/windowSeconds`.
Claims both sides stamp and both sides check. `epoch` is the per-user generation counter
behind bulk revocation: a password reset advances the stored epoch, and any token stamped
below it is rejected. A token that predates the claim reads as generation 0, which is
inert until the user's first bump. Absent from the MFA challenge token, which grants no
resource access on its own.
Optional on both sides and absent by default, so an existing deployment is unchanged.
When configured, the value is STAMPED on every token the backend mints and REQUIRED on
every token it verifies: a token carrying the wrong issuer or audience, or none at all,
is rejected. That is the whole point — a verifier that accepts an unstamped token gives
an attacker a way to opt out of the check.
Both backends must be configured with the SAME pair or they stop accepting each other's
tokens, which is the one way this setting can split a shared deployment. It is also the
reason it is not on by default.
Turning it on invalidates the access tokens already in flight, because they were minted
without the claims. The window is one access-token lifetime and clients recover by
refreshing — the refresh token is opaque and carries no claims, so rotation is unaffected.
The client-facing payloads. These are what a consumer's TypeScript describes, so a
difference here is not a store that fails to read — it is a client that compiles against
one backend and reads `undefined` from the other. The platform login body is the trap:
the account rides under `admin`, not `user`, on both sides.

login.$comment: In cookie mode the tokens are in Set-Cookie and MUST NOT also be in the body: a refresh token in a JSON payload is one an XSS can read, which is the whole reason the cookie is HttpOnly.

platformLogin.$comment: Always bearer — a platform admin console is not a browser session — and the account key is `admin`.

me.$comment: GET /auth/me answers with the BARE user object — no `{ user }` wrapper. Pinned because its absence from this table is what let one side change shape while the other kept unwrapping a key that was no longer there: the client returned `undefined` while every other signal said authenticated, and the test that should have caught it mocked the old envelope.

passwordResetRequest.$comment: Both routes acknowledge with 200 and an empty JSON object, whether or not the account exists: a body that differed by outcome would be the enumeration oracle the 200 exists to close. Pinned as an object, not left empty, so a client that parses every success body as JSON needs no special case for these two routes.

failures.before: A failure before the account is known (the resend-cooldown store, the account lookup) answers 500 auth.internal after the floor: it is the same for every address, so it tells the caller nothing about one.
failures.after: A failure after the account is known (issuing or storing the code) is logged and the 200 acknowledgement stands: it happens only for a registered address, so a 5xx would answer the enumeration question.
failures.cooldown: The resend cooldown a request took is released when the request itself observes the failure: the account lookup, the code or token store, or a send awaited inside the request. The retry a 500 invites is then not refused for the rest of the window. A send that fails after the response has left is detached from the request and never releases it, because a release from there is a delete by key that can remove a later request's fresh cooldown. A request that fails nothing leaves the cooldown in place.
failures.floor: Every exit waits until floorMs have passed since the request began, a cooldown hit and a 500 included, so releasing the cooldown for registered accounts opens no timing difference.

$comment: Every `auth.*` code either implementation can name, in the order the catalog declares them.
The two libraries can back the same deployment, so a client switching on `error.code` must
see one vocabulary — a code present on one side only is a branch that never fires against
the other, and a code neither side emits is a branch that never fires at all.
`internalOnly` names the codes that must never reach a client. Each collapses onto a public
one — the token sentinels onto `auth.token_invalid`, the OTP sentinels onto
`auth.otp_invalid` — so a caller cannot tell 'valid until revoked' from 'never valid', or
'no record was ever written here' from 'wrong code'. They stay in the catalog because they
are real internal outcomes worth logging, and the status must collapse with the code.
$statusesComment: The HTTP status each code answers with. A client switching on `error.code` switches on
the status line first — a 4xx it retries, a 429 it backs off on, a 409 it resolves — so
the status is as much of the contract as the code string, and belongs in the same file.
It was NOT in this file until 2026-08-11, and the omission cost exactly what an ungated
field costs. Thirteen codes answered a different status on each side; `nest-auth` was the
outlier in all thirteen, because its `AuthException` defaulted the status to 401 and
omitting the argument was neither a type error nor a lint error. Five codes answered
different statuses at different throw sites within nest-auth itself — `auth.account_locked`
was 429 on login and 401 on the MFA and password-reset lockouts, so a client backing off
on 429 did not back off on the others. Both suites were green throughout: each side was
self-consistent, and neither read the other. A parity test that reads only its own side
is not a parity test.
Both implementations now derive the status from the code rather than passing it per call
site, so answering one code with two statuses is not expressible.
These are WIRE statuses — what a caller actually receives. An internal-only code
therefore carries the status of the public code it collapses onto, not one of its own:
`auth.otp_max_attempts` is 401 here because it reaches a caller as `auth.otp_invalid`,
and answering 429 for it would hand back through the status line exactly what the
collapse removes from the body — only a record that exists can reach an attempt ceiling,
so a 429 says the address was registered. rust-auth is correct here by construction
(`AuthError::http_status()` is `self.code().to_wire().http_status()`, remapping before it
reads the status); the value it keeps for the pre-wire sentinel is internal to logging
and is not what this table pins.

errorEnvelope.$comment: The body shape every auth error serializes to. `details` is present and null when the thrower supplied none. For `auth.validation`, each `details[].field` is the WIRE property name, the key the client sent in the request JSON or query (`currentPassword`, never a language-level field name), and a nested field is its dotted path with an array index as a segment (`billing.name`, `items.1.name`), never bracketed. What is normative for an `auth.validation` answer is the status, the code, the top-level message and the SET of distinct `details[].field` values for a given input; the per-entry message text and the number of entries per field are not, and a library words its own, provided no message repeats the client's value or type. An unknown request property is named by the client, so its name is repeated in the answer only when it is at most 128 code points and holds no control character; an unknown property over 128 code points, holding a control character, or empty is reported once under the field `body`, however many there are, while every other failure is still reported by its own name. The answer therefore never grows with the length of a client-chosen key and never carries a control byte.

$comment: Scoped service keys for machine callers. Both libraries must mint, parse and verify the
same key, because a deployment re-issuing keys from one backend may verify them on the other.
The vector pins the digest function and the grammar; the rest pins behaviour a client can see.

keyGrammar.parsing: split on the FIRST two separators only; the prefix and the keyId contain none, the secret may

apiKeys.digest: lowercase hex hmac-sha256 with key = pepper and message = secret, utf-8; labels and scopes are never part of the input
apiKeys.header: x-api-key by default; read from that header only, never the query string; a repeated header is malformed
verificationSteps: parse, substituting a fixed dummy keyId and dummy secret when absent or malformed
look the keyId up in the store, always
compute the digest of the secret under the pepper
compare two 32-byte buffers in constant time, against a fixed dummy digest when there is no row
only then decide: parsed AND found AND equal AND not revoked AND not expired
apiKeys.validity: a key is valid strictly before expiresAt, and not at all once revokedAt is set, on every instance and whatever instant revokedAt holds; a date that does not parse counts as lapsed
apiKeys.scopes: a key must hold ALL scopes the route declares; no wildcard and no hierarchy; the most specific declaration wins (handler over class); an empty declaration is undeclared and the route is refused

refusals.api_key_invalid: absent, malformed, unknown, wrong secret, revoked, expired — one answer, no oracle
refusals.forbidden: the route declares no scopes; refused before any credential work

apiKeys.lastUsed: advisory, coalesced per process and flushed in batches; the store write must be monotonic

note: Requests refused by the HTTP layer before any route handler ran. They answer the library's
own envelope under `auth.validation`, with the status the transport itself reports, which is
why this is a table of its own: `errorCatalog.statuses` holds ONE status per code and
`auth.validation` stays 400 there. The message is fixed per row and never repeats the
parser's text or any part of the request; `details` is null.
Detection is on the error's stable `type` and its own 4xx `status`, never on message text.
A malformed JSON body and an undecodable path reach the filter as a bare 400 whose cause is
gone, so they are recognised by having happened before a route matched.

rows.condition: malformed JSON body (body-parser type entity.parse.failed, or the bare 400 Nest makes of it; a bare string or number included), or an undecodable path, refused before routing
body-parser type entity.verify.failed, request.aborted, request.size.invalid or querystring.parse.rangeError

body-parser type charset.unsupported or encoding.unsupported, or any Content-Encoding other than identity on a library route, refused by the library itself before the handler whatever the host's body parser would have decompressed
a 400 the body parser raises with no type of its own, such as a body that claims to be compressed and is not, refused before routing

contentTypeMismatch.condition: a JSON route called with Content-Type text/plain, or with none
contentTypeMismatch.details: one entry per failed field, each naming the field and a rule message; no entry carries a request value (a field name can be a key the client sent)

note: Which library routes refuse a request body that declares a Content-Encoding other than
`identity`, answering the `transportErrors` 415 row. The scope is the same in both libraries:
a route not listed under `unchecked` or `whenBody` is strict, so a route added later is checked
until someone decides it should not be. Routes are written as `METHOD path` relative to the
route prefix. A request with no Content-Encoding, or only `identity`, is never refused.
The refusal happens before authentication and rate limiting; a refused request consumes no
`whenBody` routes accept an empty body, which takes the default DTO, so they refuse only a
request that carries one: a non-zero Content-Length or a Transfer-Encoding. A path-only or
query-only route is never checked: no request of the methods in `methodsNeverChecked` is.

$comment: Workspace invitations, shared by both libraries on one Redis. An invitation is a record keyed by
the SHA-256 of a token only the invitee's mailbox holds; the token is 32 CSPRNG bytes, 64
lowercase hex characters, and is never stored. Whoever the workspace permission `manageMembers` admits can list
every pending invitation, the inviter's id included.
Three structures and one counter. `winv:{sha256(token)}` holds the record. `winvidx:` names the
ONE live invitation of an address in a workspace by the record key it points at. `winvset:` holds the
record keys of a workspace's pending invitations, for listing and for the pending cap; a member whose
record is gone is dropped when the set is read. `winvrl:` counts the invitations one member issues,
one hour from the first.
A record is published in ONE atomic step, never in several. The step takes the record key the writer
read from the index (none for a first invitation) and writes only while the index still holds it; it
then writes the record, points the index at it, adds the record key to the set, and deletes the record
it replaces and that record's place in the set. When the workspace is at the pending cap, a first
invitation writes nothing, in the same step. A writer that read a stale index writes nothing, so no
state exists in which an index names a record that is not yet written, and two overlapping
invitations for one address leave exactly one record. An index whose record is already gone (the
record expired, or was deleted) is replaced like any other.
Every record, index and set expires `workspaces.invitationTtlSeconds` after it is written
(default 604800, at most 2592000).

member.$comment: Issued by a workspace member for a workspace that exists. `role` is a role of the workspace hierarchy.

bootstrap.$comment: Issued by the platform for the invitee to OWN a workspace that does not exist until they accept. `role` is the owner role, `workspaceId` is the id the workspace will be created with, and `workspaceName` is held in the form the create route stores it: already trimmed, 1 to 120 code points, no control character, `blank` meaning only JS `\s` whitespace. There is no inviter.

record.kind: `member` or `bootstrap`, required. A record with no kind, another kind, or any other combination of the fields above is not a record: it is read as absent and answered as `auth.invalid_invitation_token`.
record.email: the invited address, trimmed and lowercased
record.createdAt: iso8601-string; when the CURRENT token was issued, reset by a resend
record.resendCount: JSON number; 0 on the first invitation, one more on each resend or second invitation of the address
record.$comment: A value under the key that is not an object with every field of the right type reads as no record. The ordinary invite route cannot set `kind`, `workspaceName` or `workspaceId`: its body accepts only `email` and `role`, and any other property is refused.

keys.index: winvidx:{hmacSha256(hmacKey, workspaceInvitationEmail preimage)}, value: the record key `winv:{hash}`
keys.set: winvset:{hmacSha256(hmacKey, workspace subject)}, members: record keys `winv:{hash}`
keys.inviterRate: winvrl:{hmacSha256(hmacKey, workspaceInviterRate preimage)}, value: a counter whose TTL is set on the first increment only

rules.oneLiveInvitationPerAddress: Inviting an address that already has a live invitation is a resend: it mints a new token, takes the role of the new request, and retires the old record.
rules.roleCeiling: The owner role may invite to any role. Every other role invites only to a role strictly below its own, and acts on (resends, revokes, replaces) only an invitation to such a role. This is stricter than `at or below`; the owner may grant the owner role. A role outside the hierarchy is refused with 400 auth.validation naming `role`.
rules.outrankedInvitation: A resend or a revoke of an address with no live invitation, or one the actor may not act on, answers 204 and changes nothing. A second invitation the actor may not replace is refused with 403 auth.insufficient_workspace_role.
rules.alreadyMember: An address whose account has a membership of the workspace, in ANY status, is refused with 409 auth.already_member: a suspended member is still a member, and an invitation cannot reinstate one. Accepting, a caller whose existing membership is not active is answered 400 auth.invalid_invitation_token and the record is not spent.
rules.limitsAnswer: The cooldown, the resend limit, the hourly limit, the pending cap (`workspaces.maxPendingInvitationsPerWorkspace`, default 100, checked in the same step that adds the record to the set, so two writers cannot both take the last place) and a lost compare-and-set on the index are all refused with 429 auth.too_many_requests. The cooldown and the resend limit apply to a second invitation of the same address as to a resend.
rules.answers: POST invite, resend and revoke answer 204 with no body, whether or not the address has an account. The email provider is told `accountExists`.
rules.preview: POST workspaces/invitations/preview takes `{token}` of exactly 64 characters, needs no credential, and answers `{kind, workspaceName, inviterName, role, maskedEmail, accountExists}` for a member invitation and `{kind, workspaceName, role, maskedEmail, accountExists}` for a bootstrap one, where the answer is a union on `kind`, the same as the record's: `member` carries `inviterName` (a string), and `bootstrap` has NO `inviterName` field because it has no inviter. A bootstrap token previews while its workspace does not exist, and is invalid once that workspace exists and is not active. A token that never existed, expired, was withdrawn or consumed, or whose workspace is not active or whose inviter is gone, is answered with the SAME 400 auth.invalid_invitation_token, and the library performs the same repository reads in each case.
rules.tokenInEmail: A delivery failure is re-thrown without the failing text, which may quote the token.
rules.capOnReplacement: Replacing a LIVE record skips the pending cap: the set does not grow. An index naming a record that is already gone counts as a first invitation for the cap, with `resendCount` 0 and no cooldown, because the dead entry is dropped before the cap is counted. Example: at a cap of 1 with one live invitation to a@x, inviting a@x again succeeds, and a first invitation to b@x answers 429.
rules.accept: POST workspaces/invitations/accept takes `{token}` of exactly 64 characters and a signed-in caller, and answers 200 `{workspaceId, role}` where `role` is the role the caller ACTUALLY holds in the workspace afterwards: the invited role, or the role of a caller who was already a member, whose membership the invitation never changes. Decided in this order, without spending the token: the token names a record, of a known role, in the caller's tenant (else 400 auth.invalid_invitation_token); the caller's address equals the record's, compared in lowercase (else 403 auth.invitation_email_mismatch); that address is verified (else 403 auth.email_not_verified); the workspace is active and the inviter still exists, is not blocked, is in the tenant, and is an ACTIVE member whose role outranks the invited role (else 400 auth.invalid_invitation_token, whatever the reason). A bootstrap record skips the inviter and member checks and needs its workspace absent or active. Then the membership is written, and only then the record is spent.
rules.acceptOrder: The acceptance takes effect when the membership is written. Spending the record afterwards deletes the token's own record key always, and the index and the set entry only while they still name that key; a revoke or a resend that lands between the write and the spend therefore cannot undo the acceptance, and the answer is still 200. A failure before the write leaves the invitation usable; a failure after it retries into `already_member`, which counts as success. The hook event for the acceptance carries `lostConsumeRace: true` only when the spend found the index no longer naming the record.
rules.acceptSignup: POST workspaces/invitations/accept-signup takes `{token, name, password}` (token exactly 64 characters, name 2 to 100, password 8 to 128 code points) and needs no credential. Order: the record, then the inviter and workspace checks as above, then an existing account for the address (409 auth.email_already_exists, the pointer to sign in and accept as above), then the password policy and breach screen, then the account is created with a verified address and no role of its own, the membership is written, the record is spent, and the session is issued as a sign-in does. A password that is refused spends nothing. When creating the account fails and an account for the address now exists, the answer is 409 auth.email_already_exists, never a server error. When the account is created and the membership write fails, the record is NOT spent and the retry answers 409 auth.email_already_exists: the holder signs in and accepts as above. Answers 201 with the sign-in body of the configured delivery mode, plus `workspaceId` and `role`.
rules.bootstrap: A bootstrap invitation is issued by the host through a service call, with no route: the platform plane's authorization is the host's. The call returns the workspace id the invitation reserves; each call is its own invitation for its own workspace. Accepting creates the workspace and the owner membership in one repository call, then spends the record. A retry that finds the workspace already created, with this caller as its active owner, is success and spends the record. A bootstrap invitation is withdrawn by the host through a second service call keyed by that workspace id; no workspace route can reach it, because its workspace does not exist.
rules.acceptLimits: accept is limited to 10 per minute per IP and accept-signup to 5 per minute per IP; the token is 256 bits, so no per-account limit adds anything.
rules.membershipStatus: Every path that reads a membership decides its status explicitly, and only an ACTIVE membership of an ACTIVE workspace grants anything. Access, and the cache that serves it, fill and read back only an active membership. Changing a member's role and removing a member act only on an ACTIVE member; a suspended one answers 404 auth.workspace_not_found. The receiver of an ownership hand-over must be ACTIVE (400 auth.validation naming `userId`), checked before the giver's password is looked at and again by the repository's write. Leaving, and the role the acting member holds, are reached only through the workspace guard, which resolves an ACTIVE membership, so a suspended member reaches neither. Inviting an address that has a membership in any status is 409 auth.already_member, and accepting with a non-active membership is 400 auth.invalid_invitation_token: an invitation never reinstates a member.
rules.bootstrapCreate: Accepting a bootstrap invitation applies to the workspace it creates what the create route applies to a workspace an account creates for itself, except the self-serve switch: first the owner cap (`workspaces.maxWorkspacesPerUser`, counted as the workspaces the account owns with the owner role), then the host's `beforeWorkspaceCreate`, then the workspace is created. The platform has already decided that this account may own a workspace, so `allowCreate` is never consulted; the acceptance may land days after the invitation, so the cap and the hook are. A refusal by the cap answers `auth.workspace_limit_reached`, a refusal by the hook `403 auth.forbidden` with `details: [{field: 'name', message: <the hook's reason, or 'Workspace creation was refused'>}]`, and neither spends the record. The retry of an acceptance whose workspace already exists with the caller as its active owner applies neither.
rules.oauthAccept: GET oauth/{provider}?workspaceInvitation=<token> starts an OAuth flow that accepts the invitation; the token is exactly 64 characters (else 400 auth.validation) and the start answers 400 auth.invalid_invitation_token when workspaces are not enabled. The start response carries `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` and the state record gains `workspaceInvitation`, the SHA-256 of the token: the raw token is never stored, and the flow stays bound to the browser that started it by the state cookie. On the callback, before the host's `onOAuthLogin` hook runs, the record is read by that hash and must be a record of a known role in the flow's tenant (else 400 auth.invalid_invitation_token); the provider's address must equal the record's, compared in lowercase (else 403 auth.invitation_email_mismatch); the provider must report that address verified (else 403 auth.email_not_verified); and the workspace and inviter must still stand, as for accept. Then the hook decides create, link or reject as for any OAuth sign-in, and the account it resolves must be the invited address, in the invitation's tenant, and verified. An account with a second factor is sent to the MFA challenge and the invitation is neither completed nor spent: its holder completes the challenge and accepts as a signed-in account. Otherwise the record is read again and the inviter's standing and the workspace are judged again immediately before the write, because the host's hook and the account write ran since the vetting: a record revoked, replaced by a resend or expired in that time, an inviter who no longer stands and a workspace that is no longer active all answer 400 auth.invalid_invitation_token with nothing written or spent; then the membership is written, the record is spent and the sign-in is delivered as for any OAuth sign-in. A bootstrap invitation applies the owner cap and `beforeWorkspaceCreate` as in `bootstrapCreate`. No refusal spends the record, and a refusal after the hook created the account leaves that account created, as for accept-signup. A refusal is delivered as every other callback failure is and never carries the token. #298 section 6 says the library links an existing account "when oauth.linkByVerifiedEmail is enabled": there is no such option, the host's `onOAuthLogin` hook decides whether to link.
rules.oauthAcceptMfa: An account with a second factor that signs in through an OAuth invitation receives the MFA challenge exactly as any OAuth sign-in does, and the invitation is neither completed nor spent: OAuth proves the mailbox and the provider account, not the second factor, and a membership is a privilege. Its holder completes the challenge and then accepts with POST workspaces/invitations/accept as a signed-in account, which spends the record as for any signed-in acceptance. A reader that completed the invitation before the challenge would grant a membership to a session that never passed the second factor.
rules.registration: `registration: 'invitation-only'` closes the self sign-up paths. POST register answers 403 auth.registration_closed before anything else is read or run, and the OAuth `create` action answers it unless the flow carries an invitation that passed the checks in `oauthAccept`. Signing in an existing account, linking an identity and every accept route are unaffected. Startup refuses the mode when `workspaces.enabled` and `invitations.enabled` are both false, naming both, since no account could ever be created.
rules.afterAcceptedHook: The host's after-acceptance hook runs when an acceptance CREATED the account: on accept-signup, on an OAuth acceptance whose flow created the account, and on the tenant invitation's accept. It does not run on the signed-in accept, nor on an OAuth acceptance that signed in an account that already existed. It is detached: neither a rejection nor a synchronous throw changes the answer, because the account, the membership, the spend and the session are already done. A failing hook is logged without its message.

$comment: Names scoped to a workspace: the keys, rooms and prefixes a host builds for storage, cache,
sockets and queues. Shared by both libraries because the same name must come out of either.
name = concatenation, for the tenant, the workspace and then every part in order, of
`<byte length>:<text>`, where the length is the number of UTF-8 bytes of the text in canonical
decimal (no leading zero, `0` for the empty text). A length-prefixed piece is self-delimiting,
so no text can move a boundary: two different argument lists never produce one name.
Refused (TypeError in nest-auth, an error in the sibling): a piece holding a C0 control
(U+0000 to U+001F) or DEL (U+007F), because several storage backends reject or mangle them;
an unpaired surrogate, which has no UTF-8 form so two different strings would write the same
bytes; an empty tenant or workspace. An empty part is allowed and is a piece of its own.
A vector with `unpairedSurrogateCodeUnits` is one more final part, built from those UTF-16 code
units, because the JSON text itself must stay well-formed.

vectors.case: an empty part is a piece of its own
vectors.name: 2:t12:w10:

vectors.case: a colon and digits inside a part
vectors.name: 2:t12:w14:2:ab

vectors.case: the same text split differently is a different name, first split
vectors.name: 2:t12:w11:a3:1:b

vectors.case: the same text split differently is a different name, second split
vectors.name: 2:t12:w13:a:11:b

vectors.name: 2:t12:w111:files/a.png
