$comment: Authorization of a workspace on the surfaces that have no route guard in front of them: streams, sockets and queued jobs. Shared by both libraries because a member removed or a workspace hidden on one must be refused and hidden on the other.

rules.accessDecision: Every surface that admits a caller to a workspace (the route guard, the stream's access verifier, a socket message) judges the resolved access in one fixed order and answers the same codes: not an active member of an active workspace, and any non-owner of a workspace pending deletion, answer the IDENTICAL 404 auth.workspace_not_found, decided from the rows already read; the OWNER of a workspace pending deletion answers 409 auth.workspace_pending_deletion unless the surface admits pending workspaces (a route's explicit decorator, a stream's allowPending), in which case only that owner is admitted; then the role is judged through the hierarchy (403 auth.insufficient_workspace_role). A surface never tells a non-owner more than the route does.
rules.workspaceIdField: A workspace id taken from a path parameter, a message body or a job context is 1 to 128 code points, not blank, with no control character; anything else answers 400 auth.validation naming `workspaceId` (`tenantId` and `actorUserId` for a job context), ahead of any lookup. A well-formed id that names nothing answers the identical 404 of accessDecision.
rules.verifierWorkspace: The access verifier takes an optional `workspace: {workspaceId, roles, allowPending}` and, on the dashboard plane, returns the caller's membership `{tenantId, workspaceId, userId, role}` beside the verified payload, resolved through the same versioned access cache as the routes (so a removal is refused within the cache's own bound) and judged by accessDecision after the identity checks. On the platform plane, or with workspaces disabled, the option is a programmer error, not an auth failure.
rules.socketMessage: A socket message is admitted to the workspace it names after the connection's identity was verified: the workspace comes from the message body (`workspaceId`, or the host's resolver given the body and nothing else), never from the URL, a header, the handshake or the ticket, which carries an identity only. Every message is judged again, so a member removed between two messages is refused on the second. The membership an admitted message earned is kept with that message and handed to its own handler, never held on the connection, because messages overlap on one connection and a single slot would let a handler act in the workspace another message was admitted to. A message that is not an object cannot carry a workspace and answers 400 auth.validation naming `workspaceId`. A handler that declares no roles is refused 403 auth.forbidden before anything is looked up, and a connection with no verified dashboard identity 401 auth.token_invalid.
rules.jobAuthorization: A queued job carries `{tenantId, workspaceId, actorUserId}` and nothing about the role. Before any side effect the worker asks whether the actor may act NOW: the account (`auth.token_invalid` when it is gone, the blocked status's own code, `auth.email_not_verified` when verification is required), the workspace and the membership are all read from the repositories on the primary, never from the access cache or the status cache, the account first, then accessDecision. It costs three repository reads per call. A workspaceId read from a job payload is never trusted without it. The check does not emit access.denied.
rules.accessDeniedEvents: A refusal of a workspace access decision on a route, on a stream verification and on a socket message is reported to the host's workspace-event hook as `access.denied`, never for the queued-job check, and never for a request refused before the decision (a malformed workspace id, a missing identity). The event carries `{type, tenantId, workspaceId, actorUserId, userId, surface, code, reason, suppressedCount, at}`: `surface` is `http`, `verifier` or `ws`; `code` is the public code the caller was answered with (`auth.workspace_not_found`, `auth.workspace_pending_deletion` or `auth.insufficient_workspace_role`), and `reason` is what the host alone is told, taken from the access decision and not from the code: `not_member` when the caller is not an active member (it covers a workspace that does not exist, which the resolution does not tell apart from one the caller does not belong to, and an inactive one), `pending_deletion` whenever the workspace is pending deletion and the caller is an active member of it, the owner (who is answered `auth.workspace_pending_deletion`) and a non-owner (who is answered `auth.workspace_not_found`, identical to a stranger) alike, and `insufficient_role` for a member below the role (`auth.insufficient_workspace_role`); so `code` and `reason` differ exactly where the disclosure rule hides the state from the caller, and a caller who is not a member of a pending workspace is `not_member`; the caller never receives the event, so `reason` discloses nothing to it; there is no role set. `actorUserId` and `userId` are always equal on these surfaces (the verified account); `at` is an ISO-8601 UTC instant as a string, `Date.prototype.toISOString`. Only a dashboard account is reported: the subject is the dashboard arm, so a platform administrator, which has no tenant, is not. The workspace id is the one the caller named, reported only after it validated. Emission is detached and never changes or delays the answer. It is bounded per account, the tenant and the user together: the subject is `dashboard:<utf8 byte length of tenantId>:<tenantId>:<userId>`, its HMAC-SHA256 under the identifier key is `<digest>`, and the window counter is the key `wad:<digest>`, incremented on every denial with its expiry set to `windowSeconds` by the increment that creates it, the increment and the expiry being ONE atomic step (a script, never two commands: a crash between them would leave a counter that never expires and an account that never emits again) (a fixed window). At most `max` events are emitted per window; a denial beyond it is not emitted but increments the key `wads:<digest>`, whose expiry is 86400 seconds, set by the increment that creates it in the same atomic step; the count is lost if no further event is emitted for the account within those 86400 seconds. The next event that is emitted reads and deletes `wads:<digest>` in one atomic step and carries the value as `suppressedCount` (0 when absent). The two keys are two slots: only the order matters, and a lost increment can only under-count. The options are `workspaces.accessDeniedEvents: {max, windowSeconds}`, positive integers, defaults `max` 10 and `windowSeconds` 60, `max` at most 10000 and `windowSeconds` at most 3600 so the suppressed count always outlives a window; startup validation raises an error whose first sentence is `workspaces.accessDeniedEvents.max must be an integer from 1 to 10000.` or `workspaces.accessDeniedEvents.windowSeconds must be an integer from 1 to 3600.`, and `workspaces.accessDeniedEvents must be an object.` for a value that is not an object. `accessDeniedVectors` pins the two keys for two accounts, including one whose tenant id holds the delimiter. When the counter store fails nothing is emitted, never an unbounded stream, one warning per window per process says so, and the access decision is unchanged. An allowed request never touches either key. One budget covers all three surfaces of an account.
rules.workspaceScopedName: Rooms, cache keys and storage prefixes a host builds for a workspace use the `workspaceScopedName` encoding declared in its own section, so two workspaces cannot collide on a delimiter.

$comment: Removing every membership of an account that the host is about to delete or anonymise. Shared by both libraries because a workspace left without an owner, or a membership left behind, is the same defect whichever library the deployment runs.

rules.scope: The removal covers every membership of the account in the tenant, in every membership status (active or suspended) and in every workspace status, not only the active memberships of active workspaces that the workspace picker lists. Only the repository can enumerate them all, so it is one port call (`removeAllForUser`) that the host makes before deleting or anonymising the user; the library never deletes a user and wires nothing automatically.
rules.blocking: The removal is refused, with nothing written, no audit row and no cache change, while the account is the only ACTIVE holder of the owner role of a workspace whose status is `active` or `suspended`. The refusal is 409 auth.last_owner with `details.workspaces` naming each blocking workspace as `{id, name, status}` (at most 100), or as `{id}` alone when the repository found it during the write (see atomicity). The host transfers ownership or schedules the workspace's deletion first.
rules.pendingDeletion: A workspace whose status is `pending_deletion` never blocks, and neither does a `deleted` one. No one can finalize a pending deletion before its grace period ends, so an owner who scheduled a deletion would otherwise be unable to delete their own account for the whole period. The account's membership there is removed with the others, so the workspace has no owner and can no longer be restored (restoring is owner-only); it is deleted when its grace period ends, which needs no member.
rules.atomicity: The last-owner decision and every removal are one transaction in the repository, which re-decides the blocking rule inside it: a workspace that became solely owned by the account after the library's own read refuses the whole call with `last_owner` and the ids of those workspaces, and nothing is removed. The library reads the sole-owned workspaces first only to name them to the caller.
rules.audit: One `member.removed` event is persisted per removed membership in the same transaction, `{type, tenantId, workspaceId, actorUserId, userId, at}`, where `actorUserId` is the account itself, an administrator, or null for a job, and `at` is one ISO-8601 UTC instant for the whole call. The same events are reported to the host's workspace-event hook after the commit, detached and best-effort.
rules.cache: After the commit the cached access of every removed membership is dropped by bumping that membership's version, so access ends at the next request, the same bound as a single removal. Every bump is attempted even when one fails. If any fails the call fails with the full removed list and the failed list: the removal is already committed, so repeating the call finds nothing to remove, and the host drops the failed ones through the access service's `invalidateMembership` or waits out `membershipCacheTtlSeconds`.

workspaceOwnerRole.$comment: The name of the OWNER role of `workspaces.roles` (`ownerRole`), and no other role of the hierarchy: other role names keep whatever shape a host gives them. The owner role is refused at startup, naming the option and the value, unless it is 1 to `maxLength` code points of well-formed text with no control character (the C0 and C1 ranges and DEL): the rule an id follows, and no charset. A code point is counted once, an emoji included. The role is part of the key of a `listSoleOwned` cursor, and its length is what keeps that cursor under the cursor bound of `requestFieldBounds.pageLimit`: with the longest role of the costliest characters the longest cursor of nest-auth's format is 2306 characters. Each `refuses` entry is the string `value`, with the code units of `unpairedSurrogateCodeUnits` appended when it has them, so no ill-formed string appears in this file.

refuses.case: an unpaired low surrogate after a letter
